questions.question: What is the primary difference between a CROSS JOIN and an INNER JOIN?
questions.title: CROSS JOIN vs INNER JOIN
options: INNER JOIN returns the Cartesian product; CROSS JOIN filters rows on a condition
They are identical; only the keyword differs
CROSS JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both tables; INNER JOIN does not
CROSS JOIN pairs every row with every row; INNER JOIN keeps only rows matching the join condition
questions.answer: CROSS JOIN pairs every row with every row; INNER JOIN keeps only rows matching the join condition

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of two tables — every row of table A paired with every row of table B, with no join condition. An INNER JOIN also starts conceptually from that Cartesian product but then filters it using an ON condition, keeping only the row pairs that satisfy the condition.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: CROSS JOIN returns all possible row combinations (m × n rows) unconditionally, while INNER JOIN returns only the combinations that satisfy a specified matching condition between the tables.

questions.question: Which relational algebra operation is most suitable for answering queries like "Find the names of sailors who have reserved ALL boats"?
questions.title: Relational algebra for "sailors who reserved ALL boats"
options: Natural join (⋈)
Division (÷)
Selection (σ)
Projection (π)
questions.answer: Division (÷)

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Queries containing the word "ALL" (universal quantification) map to the **division (÷)** operator in relational algebra. Division of Reserves(sid, bid) by Boats(bid) gives all sid values that are paired with every bid in Boats.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **Division operator**. Step: Divide Reserves(sid,bid) ÷ πbid(Boats) to get sailors whose reserved-boat set is a superset of the full boat set.

questions.question: In extendible hashing architectures utilized for dynamic database indexing, what directly dictates the total number of primary bucket pointers actively maintained within the main global directory array?
questions.title: Extendible hashing — bucket pointers
options: The local depth of each bucket
The number of records stored
The global depth of the directory
The bucket capacity (page size)
questions.answer: The global depth of the directory

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Extendible hashing keeps a global directory of 2^(global depth) pointers, where "global depth" (d) is the number of leading bits of the hash used to index the directory. Multiple directory entries can point to the same bucket if that bucket's local depth is less than the global depth.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **global depth (d) of the directory** — the number of bits used for indexing — directly determines the number of pointers: there are always 2^d pointer slots in the directory.

questions.question: During the execution of the ARIES database recovery algorithm following a system crash, what is the explicit primary objective of the initial "Analysis" phase before any data modifications occur?
questions.title: ARIES recovery — Analysis phase
options: Reapply all logged updates to disk
Flush all dirty pages and truncate the log
Roll back all uncommitted transactions
Find the transactions active and pages dirty at the time of the crash
questions.answer: Find the transactions active and pages dirty at the time of the crash

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: ARIES recovery has three phases: Analysis, Redo, Undo. Analysis scans forward from the last checkpoint through the log.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The Analysis phase's objective is to **determine which transactions were active (uncommitted) at the time of the crash and which pages were dirty**, rebuilding the Transaction Table and Dirty Page Table so Redo knows where to start and Undo knows what to roll back.

questions.question: In log-based recovery, what must happen before a transaction is allowed to commit?
questions.title: Log-based recovery — commit rule
options: All locks held by other transactions must be released
A checkpoint must be taken
All modified data pages must be written to disk
All its log records, including the commit record, must be flushed to stable storage
questions.answer: All its log records, including the commit record, must be flushed to stable storage

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: This is the **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** rule.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Before a transaction commits, **all its log records (including the commit record) must be flushed to stable/non-volatile storage**, ensuring the transaction's effects can be redone even after a crash.

questions.question: What is the primary structural vulnerability associated with utilizing a Dense Index architecture on a highly volatile database table experiencing massive volumes of concurrent INSERT and DELETE operations?
questions.title: Dense Index — vulnerability under heavy INSERT/DELETE
options: It requires the data file to be unsorted
Every insert or delete forces an index update, causing heavy maintenance overhead
It stores one entry per block, making lookups slow
It cannot support range queries
questions.answer: Every insert or delete forces an index update, causing heavy maintenance overhead

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: A dense index has one index entry per record. Every insert/delete of a data record forces a corresponding insert/delete in the index itself.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: High **maintenance overhead** — the index must be updated on every single insert/delete, causing excessive I/O and making it inefficient for volatile tables, unlike a sparse index which only tracks block-level entries.

questions.question: A relational database table schema is definitively classified as being in the Fourth Normal Form (4NF) if and only if it is already in Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) and fundamentally strictly prohibits the existence of:
questions.title: 4NF definition
options: Repeating groups of attributes
Transitive dependencies on non-prime attributes
Partial functional dependencies
Non-trivial multi-valued dependencies
questions.answer: Non-trivial multi-valued dependencies

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: 4NF builds on BCNF by additionally eliminating multi-valued dependencies (MVDs) that aren't functional dependencies.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: 4NF requires BCNF **plus the absence of non-trivial multi-valued dependencies (other than a dependency on a superkey)** — i.e., no two or more independent multi-valued facts about the same entity coexist in one relation.

questions.question: In hashing, the technique of resolving collisions by searching sequentially for the next available empty slot in the hash table is called:
questions.title: Collision resolution by sequential search
options: Separate chaining
Linear probing
Double hashing
Quadratic probing
questions.answer: Linear probing

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: When a hash collision occurs, the system searches consecutive slots until it finds an empty one.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This technique is called **Linear Probing**, a form of open addressing.

questions.question: If a relation possesses the functional dependencies {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D}, what represents the mathematically complete closure of the specified attribute set {A}+?
questions.title: Attribute closure {A}+
options: {A, B}
{A, B, C, D}
{B, C, D}
questions.answer: {A, B, C, D}

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Given A→B, B→C, C→D, closure computation repeatedly applies FDs: start with {A}, add B (from A→B), then C (from B→C), then D (from C→D).

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: {A}+ = **{A, B, C, D}** (the full attribute set), since A transitively determines every other attribute.

questions.question: What is the cardinality ratio of a relationship where one instance of entity A is associated with at most one instance of entity B, and vice versa?
questions.title: Cardinality ratio — at most one on both sides
options: 1:N (one-to-many)
M:N (many-to-many)
1:1 (one-to-one)
N:1 (many-to-one)
questions.answer: 1:1 (one-to-one)

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Cardinality ratios describe max participation: 1:1, 1:N, M:N.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This is a **1:1 (one-to-one)** relationship — each entity in A relates to at most one in B and vice versa.

questions.question: According to the Augmentation rule of Armstrong's Axioms, if the functional dependency X -> Y holds, then for any set of attributes Z:
questions.title: Armstrong's Axioms — Augmentation rule
options: X → Z
XZ → YZ
Z → XY
Y → X
questions.answer: XZ → YZ

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Augmentation states that adding the same attributes to both sides of a valid FD preserves the dependency.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: If X → Y holds, then **XZ → YZ** holds for any attribute set Z.

questions.question: In an ER diagram, an attribute that can have multiple values for a single entity (e.g., a person's phone numbers) is represented by:
questions.title: Multi-valued attribute in ER diagram
options: A double oval
A rectangle with a double border
A dashed oval
A single oval with underlined name
questions.answer: A double oval

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Standard ER notation uses different shapes to distinguish attribute types (simple = single oval, composite = oval with sub-ovals, derived = dashed oval).

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A multi-valued attribute is represented by a **double oval (double-bordered ellipse)**.

questions.question: In a standard B+ Tree index structure deployed within a relational database, what is the primary fundamental characteristic that distinguishes its internal routing nodes from its leaf nodes?
questions.title: B+ Tree — internal vs leaf nodes
options: Internal nodes are linked in a list; leaf nodes are not
Internal nodes hold data records; leaf nodes hold only keys
Internal nodes hold only routing keys; leaf nodes hold the records/pointers and are linked together
Both node types store identical data
questions.answer: Internal nodes hold only routing keys; leaf nodes hold the records/pointers and are linked together

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: In a B+ Tree, all actual data records (or pointers to them) reside only at the leaf level; internal nodes exist purely to guide the search.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Internal nodes store **only routing/index keys used to direct search paths** (no actual data), while **leaf nodes store the actual data pointers/records and are linked together sequentially** for efficient range queries.

questions.question: In the context of database transaction isolation, which specific concurrency phenomenon is uniquely prevented by the "SERIALIZABLE" isolation level but remains theoretically possible under the "REPEATABLE READ" isolation level?
questions.title: Isolation levels — SERIALIZABLE vs REPEATABLE READ
options: Non-repeatable reads
Dirty writes
Phantom reads
Dirty reads
questions.answer: Phantom reads

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: The four standard anomalies (in increasing severity) are: Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, Phantom Read, Serialization Anomaly. REPEATABLE READ prevents the first two but not phantoms; SERIALIZABLE prevents all.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Phantom Reads** are prevented only by SERIALIZABLE; they remain possible under REPEATABLE READ.

questions.question: In Tuple Relational Calculus (TRC), what critical mathematical concept ensures that a formulated query is inherently "safe" and will definitively generate a finite result set rather than an infinite domain of values?
questions.title: TRC — safety of a query
options: Using only the universal quantifier ∀
Restricting query results to values drawn from the database's own finite domain
Declaring all tuple variables as free
Allowing negation over unrestricted variables
questions.answer: Restricting query results to values drawn from the database's own finite domain

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: An "unsafe" TRC query could reference values outside the domain of the database (e.g., using negation over an infinite domain), yielding a potentially infinite result.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The concept is **the domain of the query being restricted to values that actually appear in the database (or its constants)** — this restriction to a finite, bounded domain guarantees safety and a finite result set.

questions.question: Which property of a transaction schedule ensures that if a transaction fails, it does not require the rollback of other already committed transactions?
questions.title: Cascadeless schedules
options: Schedules allowing dirty reads
Schedules that avoid all locking
Cascadeless (avoids cascading rollback) schedule
Non-recoverable schedule
questions.answer: Cascadeless (avoids cascading rollback) schedule

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Cascading rollback occurs when an uncommitted transaction's write is read by another transaction, forcing both to roll back if the first fails.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This is called the **Cascadeless (Avoids Cascading Rollback) property** — transactions may only read values written by already-committed transactions.

questions.question: Under the basic Timestamp Ordering protocol, what happens if a transaction attempts to write a data item that has a larger read timestamp than the transaction's own timestamp?
questions.title: Timestamp Ordering — write with larger read timestamp
options: The write is allowed and the read timestamp is updated
The write is silently ignored and the transaction continues
The write is delayed until the reader commits
The write is rejected and the transaction is rolled back
questions.answer: The write is rejected and the transaction is rolled back

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: In basic TO protocol, Ti wants to write item Q. If RTS(Q) > TS(Ti), a younger transaction already read Q's older value, so this write would violate serializability.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The write is **rejected and Ti is rolled back (aborted)**, since a transaction with a later timestamp has already read the value the write would overwrite.

questions.question: Which database normal form is exclusively concerned with the identification and resolution of multi-valued dependencies?
questions.title: Normal form for multi-valued dependencies
options: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
Third Normal Form (3NF)
Second Normal Form (2NF)
Fourth Normal Form (4NF)
questions.answer: Fourth Normal Form (4NF)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Fourth Normal Form (4NF)** deals specifically with eliminating non-trivial multi-valued dependencies.

questions.question: In the Wait-Die deadlock prevention scheme based on transaction timestamps, what is the deterministic outcome if a newer (younger) transaction requests a database lock that is currently held by an older transaction?
questions.title: Wait-Die scheme — younger requests lock held by older
options: Both transactions are aborted
The younger transaction is aborted (dies) and restarted later
The younger transaction waits for the older one
The older transaction is aborted
questions.answer: The younger transaction is aborted (dies) and restarted later

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Wait-Die: "older waits, younger dies." If Ti (requesting) is older than Tj (holding), Ti waits. If Ti is younger, Ti is aborted (dies).

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Since the requesting transaction is younger than the holder, it is **aborted (dies)** and restarted later with the same original timestamp.

questions.question: What does the acronym BASE stand for in the context of NoSQL database properties?
questions.title: BASE (NoSQL)
options: Binary Access, Shared state, Immediate consistency
Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
Basically Available, Strong state, Isolated consistency
Basic Atomicity, Stable state, Eventual consistency
questions.answer: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: BASE stands for **Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent** — the relaxed-consistency counterpart to the ACID model, favoring availability over strict consistency.

questions.question: Consider a transaction schedule involving operations from multiple concurrent transactions. A schedule is strictly defined as conflict serializable if and only if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping:
questions.title: Conflict serializability — swap operations
options: Consecutive non-conflicting operations
Commit operations only
Any two operations of the same transaction
Consecutive conflicting operations
questions.answer: Consecutive non-conflicting operations

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A schedule is conflict serializable if it can be converted to a serial schedule by swapping **consecutive non-conflicting operations** (operations from different transactions on different data items, or reads on the same item — any pair that doesn't affect each other's outcome if reordered).

questions.question: What is a key characteristic of a Sparse Index?
questions.title: Sparse Index — key characteristic
options: One index entry for every record
It stores no pointers to data blocks
It works only on unsorted files
One index entry per data block, with the file sorted on the key
questions.answer: One index entry per data block, with the file sorted on the key

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Unlike a dense index, a sparse index has one entry per data block (not per record), and requires the data file to be sorted on the indexed field.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A sparse index contains **one index entry per block/page rather than per record**, requiring the underlying file to be physically sorted on the index key — this makes it smaller but requires scanning within a block to find a specific record.

questions.question: The primary purpose of taking a 'Checkpoint' in database recovery management is to:
questions.title: Purpose of a Checkpoint
options: Remove the need for write-ahead logging
Reduce recovery time by limiting how much of the log must be examined
Increase the size of the log
Prevent all transaction failures
questions.answer: Reduce recovery time by limiting how much of the log must be examined

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A checkpoint's purpose is to **reduce recovery time** by periodically flushing all committed changes and in-memory state to disk, so that after a crash, the recovery process only needs to examine the log from the most recent checkpoint onward rather than from the beginning.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between DROP TABLE and DELETE FROM table?
questions.title: DROP TABLE vs DELETE FROM
options: DROP removes only rows; DELETE removes the table structure
DROP can use a WHERE clause; DELETE cannot
Both remove the structure, but DELETE is slower
DROP removes the table structure and data; DELETE removes only rows
questions.answer: DROP removes the table structure and data; DELETE removes only rows

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: DROP is a DDL command; DELETE is a DML command.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: DROP TABLE **removes the entire table structure, its data, indexes, and constraints permanently** (and cannot generally be rolled back once committed), while DELETE FROM **only removes rows (data) from the table**, keeping the table structure intact, and can be filtered with a WHERE clause and rolled back within a transaction.

questions.question: Which of the following SQL commands executed by Transaction T1 will most likely result in a Phantom Read anomaly if Transaction T2 concurrently executes an INSERT operation, assuming the isolation level permits it?
questions.title: Phantom Read scenario
options: T1 reads the same row twice and sees an updated value
T1 reads a row that T2 changed but has not committed
T1 and T2 update the same row and one update is lost
T1 runs the same range SELECT twice while T2 inserts a matching row
questions.answer: T1 runs the same range SELECT twice while T2 inserts a matching row

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: A phantom read occurs when a transaction re-executes a range query and finds new rows that another transaction inserted in between.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: T1 executing a **range-based SELECT (e.g., SELECT ... WHERE condition) twice** within the same transaction, while T2 concurrently INSERTs a new row matching that condition, causes a phantom read — T1's second read sees a row that "appeared out of nowhere."

questions.question: In the context of Enhanced ER (EER) modeling, what does a disjointness constraint specify in a specialization hierarchy?
questions.title: EER — disjointness constraint
options: Whether every superclass entity must belong to some subclass
Whether an entity can belong to more than one subclass (disjoint vs overlapping)
Whether a subclass may have its own attributes
Whether subclasses inherit the superclass key
questions.answer: Whether an entity can belong to more than one subclass (disjoint vs overlapping)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A disjointness constraint specifies **whether the subclasses in a specialization can overlap** — "disjoint" means an entity instance can belong to only one subclass, while "overlapping" (non-disjoint) allows an entity to belong to more than one subclass simultaneously.

questions.question: A Superkey is defined as:
questions.title: Superkey definition
options: A foreign key referencing another relation
A minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple
An attribute set that determines no other attribute
Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple
questions.answer: Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A Superkey is **any set of one or more attributes that, taken collectively, uniquely identifies a tuple in a relation** (it may contain extra, non-essential attributes — unlike a candidate key, which is minimal).

questions.question: In the strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) protocol, what specific operational rule is enforced to absolutely guarantee that the resulting transaction schedule is completely free of cascading rollbacks?
questions.title: Strict 2PL — avoiding cascading rollbacks
options: Shared locks are never used
All locks are acquired only after commit
Exclusive locks are held until the transaction commits or aborts
Locks are released immediately after each operation
questions.answer: Exclusive locks are held until the transaction commits or aborts

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Strict 2PL enforces the rule that **all exclusive (write) locks held by a transaction are released only after the transaction commits or aborts** (not before). This ensures no other transaction can read an uncommitted write, eliminating cascading rollbacks entirely.

questions.question: A relation is in Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) if and only if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y:
questions.title: BCNF definition
options: X is a superkey
X is a proper subset of a candidate key
Y is a prime attribute
Y is a subset of X
questions.answer: X is a superkey

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A relation is in BCNF if for every non-trivial FD X → Y, **X must be a superkey of the relation** (there is no requirement about Y being prime, unlike 3NF).

questions.question: In the Wound-Wait deadlock prevention scheme, what occurs if an older transaction requests a lock currently held by a younger transaction?
questions.title: Wound-Wait — older requests lock held by younger
options: Both continue without locking
The older transaction is aborted
The older transaction waits for the younger to finish
The older transaction wounds (aborts) the younger one and takes the lock
questions.answer: The older transaction wounds (aborts) the younger one and takes the lock

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Wound-Wait: "older wounds (preempts), younger waits."

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The older transaction **"wounds" (forces the abort of) the younger transaction** holding the lock, and then acquires the lock itself. If the situation were reversed (younger requesting from older), the younger transaction would simply wait.

questions.question: In an ER diagram, how is a derived attribute typically represented?
questions.title: Derived attribute representation
options: A double oval
A diamond
A single solid oval
A dashed oval
questions.answer: A dashed oval

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A derived attribute is represented by a **dashed/dotted oval (ellipse)** in an ER diagram, since its value can be computed from other attributes (e.g., Age derived from Date of Birth).

questions.question: How is a multi-valued attribute typically mapped from an ER diagram to a relational schema?
questions.title: Mapping multi-valued attribute to relational schema
options: As a derived column computed at query time
As a separate table holding the entity's primary key plus the attribute
As one column holding comma-separated values
As repeated columns (attr1, attr2, ...) in the same table
questions.answer: As a separate table holding the entity's primary key plus the attribute

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A multi-valued attribute is mapped to a **separate relation/table**, containing the primary key of the original entity plus the multi-valued attribute itself, with the combination forming the new table's primary key (this allows multiple rows per entity instance).

questions.question: What is the primary function of a database cursor?
questions.title: Purpose of a database cursor
options: Store the result permanently as a new table
Enforce referential integrity
Process a query's result set one row at a time
Speed up queries through an index
questions.answer: Process a query's result set one row at a time

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A cursor is a control structure that enables **row-by-row traversal and processing of the result set of a query**, allowing sequential fetch, update, or delete operations on individual rows rather than treating the result as a single set.

questions.question: Which level of the three-tier database architecture defines how the data is actually stored physically on the hardware disk, including indexing and access paths?
questions.title: Three-tier architecture — physical storage level
options: Application level
Internal (physical) level
External (view) level
Conceptual (logical) level
questions.answer: Internal (physical) level

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This is the **Internal (Physical) level** — it describes how data is actually stored on disk, including file organization, indexing structures, and access paths, hidden from users at higher levels.

questions.question: For a relation decomposition to be lossless, a fundamental requirement is that the common attribute(s) between the decomposed relations must be:
questions.title: Lossless decomposition — requirement on common attributes
options: A superkey of at least one of the decomposed relations
A multi-valued attribute
Absent from both relations
A non-prime attribute in both relations
questions.answer: A superkey of at least one of the decomposed relations

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: For lossless-join decomposition, the common attribute(s) between the two decomposed relations **must form a superkey (candidate key) of at least one of the two resulting relations** — i.e., the common attribute set must functionally determine all attributes of one of the relations.

questions.question: In Relational Algebra, which operator is used to select specific columns (attributes) from a relation?
questions.title: Relational Algebra — selecting columns
options: Union (∪)
Rename (ρ)
Selection (σ)
Projection (π)
questions.answer: Projection (π)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The **Projection (π)** operator selects specific columns/attributes from a relation (as opposed to Selection σ, which filters rows).

questions.question: The conceptual level of database architecture primarily describes:
questions.title: Conceptual level of database architecture
options: The application programs that access the database
The logical structure of the whole database, independent of physical storage
How data is physically stored on disk
One user's customized view of the data
questions.answer: The logical structure of the whole database, independent of physical storage

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The conceptual level describes the **overall logical structure of the entire database for the whole community of users** — entities, relationships, constraints — independent of physical storage details and independent of any individual user's view.

questions.question: If relation R has 'm' tuples and relation S has 'n' tuples, what is the maximum number of tuples that the Cartesian product (R x S) will contain?
questions.title: Cartesian product size
options: max(m, n)
m − n
m + n
m × n
questions.answer: m × n

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: R × S pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The maximum number of tuples is **m × n**.

questions.question: What does the "degree" of a relationship refer to in the context of an ER diagram?
questions.title: Degree of a relationship
options: The maximum cardinality ratio
The number of attributes of the relationship
The number of entity types participating in the relationship
The number of instances of each entity
questions.answer: The number of entity types participating in the relationship

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The degree of a relationship refers to **the number of entity types (entity sets) participating in that relationship** (e.g., binary = 2, ternary = 3).

questions.question: Within an advanced SQL relational database system, what is the fundamental functional restriction imposed on an AFTER trigger when directly compared to an INSTEAD OF trigger?
questions.title: AFTER trigger vs INSTEAD OF trigger restriction
options: It runs before constraints are checked
It can replace the triggering statement before it runs
It can be defined only on views
It fires after the operation, so it cannot replace the triggering statement
questions.answer: It fires after the operation, so it cannot replace the triggering statement

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: An AFTER trigger **cannot modify the data of the triggering statement before it is applied** — it fires only after the original operation (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) has already completed, so it cannot replace or prevent the base operation the way an INSTEAD OF trigger can (which runs in place of the operation).

questions.question: What is a domain in the context of the relational data model?
questions.title: Domain in relational model
options: A set of candidate keys
The number of attributes in a relation
The set of valid atomic values an attribute may take
A set of tuples in a relation
questions.answer: The set of valid atomic values an attribute may take

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A domain is **the set of all valid/permissible atomic values that an attribute can take** — essentially the data type plus the allowed range/set of values for a given column.

questions.question: A relation schema is formally in Third Normal Form (3NF) if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> A, either X is a superkey, OR:
questions.title: 3NF definition
options: A is a foreign key
A is a non-prime attribute
X is a proper subset of a candidate key
A is a prime attribute (part of some candidate key)
questions.answer: A is a prime attribute (part of some candidate key)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A relation is in 3NF if, for every non-trivial FD X → A, either X is a superkey, **or A is a prime attribute (i.e., A is part of some candidate key)**.

questions.question: What does the ACID property 'Isolation' guarantee in a DBMS transaction?
questions.title: What does the ACID property 'Isolation' guarantee in a DBMS
options: Concurrent transactions produce the same result as if executed serially
All operations in a transaction either fully complete or fully fail
Data remains valid according to all defined rules after the transaction
Once committed, changes survive even after a system crash
questions.answer: Concurrent transactions produce the same result as if executed serially

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: ACID = Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Isolation deals specifically with how concurrently running transactions interact.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Isolation guarantees that the outcome of running multiple transactions concurrently is the same as if they had been executed one after another (serially)** — intermediate, uncommitted states of one transaction are not visible to others.

questions.question: In a star schema, what is the defining structural difference between a fact table and a dimension table?
questions.title: In a star schema, what is the defining structural difference
options: Fact tables hold measurable, numeric events; dimension tables hold descriptive attributes
Fact tables are always smaller than dimension tables
Dimension tables cannot have primary keys
Fact tables never contain foreign keys
questions.answer: Fact tables hold measurable, numeric events; dimension tables hold descriptive attributes

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Star schemas are common in data warehousing (e.g., Power BI models) — a central fact table connects to multiple surrounding dimension tables.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **A fact table stores quantitative, measurable data (e.g., sales amount, quantity) tied to foreign keys of the dimensions, while dimension tables store descriptive, categorical context (e.g., product name, region, date)** used to slice and filter the facts.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the two-phase commit (2PC) protocol in distributed databases?
questions.title: What is the main purpose of the two-phase commit (2PC) proto
options: To ensure all participating nodes either commit or abort a transaction uniformly
To speed up read queries across replicas
To assign primary keys across shards
To compress log files during recovery
questions.answer: To ensure all participating nodes either commit or abort a transaction uniformly

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: 2PC coordinates a transaction spanning multiple database nodes (a coordinator + participants).

sections.label: Steps
sections.content:
1. Prepare phase: the coordinator asks all participants if they can commit; each replies yes/no.
2. Commit phase: only if ALL participants said yes does the coordinator tell everyone to commit; otherwise it tells everyone to abort.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **2PC ensures atomicity across multiple nodes — either every participating node commits the transaction, or all of them abort it**, preventing a state where some nodes committed and others didn't.
